item.title: $800-a-day penalty threatens to bleed reporter dry as explosive legal fight heads to Supreme Court
item.description: Catherine Herridge's Supreme Court petition challenges how courts weigh reporter's privilege when confidential national security sources are at stake.
item.content:encoded:
Former Fox News investigative reporter Catherine Herridge is asking the Supreme Court to protect her confidential sources after a federal court ordered her to identify who helped expose a woman's alleged ties to China's military.

The outcome of the case could dramatically reshape the legal protections afforded to journalists working in the U.S. under the First Amendment.

Herridge was held in contempt and ordered to pay $800 per day for refusing to reveal sources behind her 2017 reporting on Yanping Chen, a Chinese American businesswoman who operated a university attended by U.S. military personnel. Her reporting raised questions about Chen's alleged past as a colonel for the People's Liberation Army (PLA) of China and the potential exposure of sensitive information about American service members.

The Department of War subsequently cut off military tuition assistance funding to Chen's university following a national security review, according to a filing by Herridge's legal team. The school had been receiving approximately $200,000 a month in taxpayer-funded tuition assistance.

NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES

Now Chen, who was investigated by federal authorities but never charged with a crime, is pursuing a lawsuit against the federal government, alleging that officials improperly disclosed her private records to Herridge in violation of the Privacy Act. She has sought to compel Herridge to identify her sources as part of that litigation.

The dispute has reached the Supreme Court, where Herridge's attorneys are asking the justices to reconsider the legal standard used to force journalists to disclose confidential sources in civil cases.

Her legal team argues that the lower courts failed to adequately weigh the broader circumstances of Chen's lawsuit, including the Pentagon's national security findings and whether Chen can ultimately prevail in her claims against the government.

The case also exposes a longstanding disagreement among federal appeals courts over the scope of the reporter's privilege, an issue the Supreme Court has not comprehensively addressed in more than five decades.

Herridge's original investigation, published while she was working at Fox News in 2017, examined Chen's background and her operation of the University of Management and Technology in Arlington, Virginia, which enrolled U.S. military personnel using Defense Department tuition assistance.

The reporting included photographs appearing to show Chen in a Chinese military uniform and examined allegations that she had concealed her previous military service when applying for U.S. immigration benefits.

It also raised concerns about the university's collection of information on American service members, including details about their military training and professional backgrounds. A whistleblower interviewed for the investigation alleged that information stored on the school's computers could be accessed remotely from China.

WASHINGTON POST BOASTS IT STARED DOWN ‘UNWARRANTED’ JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUBPOENA

Federal authorities had previously investigated Chen over potential immigration violations and counterintelligence concerns, but prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia declined to bring charges.

Following Herridge's reporting, the Pentagon completed a review of Chen's university and terminated its eligibility for military tuition assistance funding, according to her filing.

Chen subsequently filed suit against the federal government, alleging that confidential information from government records had been improperly disclosed to Herridge. She contends that identifying the officials responsible for the alleged disclosures is necessary to establish her Privacy Act claims.

Herridge refused to identify her sources, arguing that compelling disclosure would undermine the ability of journalists to obtain sensitive information from government officials and whistleblowers.

A federal judge ultimately ordered Herridge to disclose the sources and held her in civil contempt when she refused. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the order, prompting her appeal to the Supreme Court.

Fox News Media has continued to support Herridge's legal fight, including covering her legal fees, despite her departure from the network in 2019.

At the center of Herridge's petition is a disagreement among federal appeals courts over how judges should evaluate a journalist's claim of privilege when confidential sources are sought in civil litigation.

The filing argues that the D.C. Circuit applied a narrow test focused primarily on whether Chen needed the information to pursue her lawsuit and whether she had exhausted alternative means of obtaining it.

They contend that courts should also consider the strength of the underlying lawsuit and the consequences of compelling disclosure, particularly when confidential national security sources may be involved.

The distinction could prove significant for journalists reporting on sensitive government matters. Under the standard challenged by Herridge, a plaintiff could obtain a reporter's confidential sources even if other deficiencies in the lawsuit would ultimately prevent the plaintiff from recovering damages, according to the petition.

item.title: What will we leave our children? The American Dream demands more than comfort
item.description: The American dream was built on generational sacrifice, but rising federal deficits and cultural retreat raise urgent questions about what we leave behind.
item.content:encoded:
As Americans prepare to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, much of the national conversation centers on which party will control Congress and what the next two years will mean for the country. Those are important questions, but a more consequential one reaches beyond the next election and our own lifetimes: What kind of America are we leaving to our children and grandchildren?

For much of our history, the American Dream was rooted in the conviction that the next generation should inherit greater freedom and opportunity than the one before it. Men and women crossed oceans, endured hardship, established communities and sacrificed their own comfort because they believed their children could enjoy opportunities they might never experience. They understood that the measure of a generation was not simply what it accumulated, but what it preserved for those who followed.

Consider the early settlers who crossed the Atlantic seeking religious freedom. They knew their journey would demand sacrifice, yet they believed the freedom to worship according to conscience was worth securing. Their convictions helped shape the American understanding that faith and conscience belong to the individual, not the government.

ARKANSAS TAKES HOME TOP RANKING FOR RELIGIOUS FREEDOM AFTER GOV SANDERS EXPANDS KEY PROTECTIONS

In his 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists, President Thomas Jefferson affirmed the constitutional protection of religious conscience against government interference. Religious liberty was never intended to remove faith from public life. It was intended to protect the right of every American to freely exercise their religious beliefs and worship without government subjugation.

Later generations of immigrants came seeking economic opportunity. They worked difficult jobs, built businesses and raised families hoping their children might achieve more than they had. Their circumstances differed from those of the early settlers, but they shared a fundamental understanding of the American Dream: sacrificing something in the present to secure something greater for the future.

SEN TIM SCOTT: MY FAMILY'S JOURNEY SHOWS AMERICA'S FOUNDING PROMISE IS ALIVE AND STRONG

Somewhere along the way, we began losing that generational perspective. The American Dream increasingly became a question of what we could acquire and enjoy during our lifetimes rather than what we could build for those who followed. We became more concerned with protecting our immediate comfort than confronting the difficult decisions necessary to preserve our children's future.

Our national finances illustrate that shift. The federal government continues operating with enormous annual deficits, adding to a national debt future generations will inherit. Reasonable people disagree over spending priorities, taxation and government's proper role. Yet every American should consider whether we are willing to make difficult decisions today or are content to pass their consequences to children who have no voice in making them.

AMERICA’S DEBT CRISIS THREATENS OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE. WE THE PEOPLE NEED TO FIX IT

This is ultimately a question of stewardship that extends far beyond government spending. A free society cannot survive indefinitely on previous generations' sacrifices while refusing to make sacrifices of its own. Religious liberty, economic opportunity, strong families and healthy communities require more than appreciation for what we inherited. They require the conviction to preserve those blessings for people we may never meet.

Christians should understand this responsibility. Scripture calls believers to care for others and pass the knowledge of God from one generation to the next. In John 13:34, Jesus commands His disciples to love one another as He has loved them. That love is demonstrated through what we are willing to give of ourselves for others.

AMERICA’S NEXT 250 YEARS DEPEND ON PASSING FAITH AND FREEDOM TO OUR CHILDREN

Yet I wonder whether we have become so accustomed to inherited freedoms that we have forgotten what preserving them requires. Previous generations endured persecution and extraordinary hardship to secure religious liberty. Today, Christians sometimes hesitate to express their convictions because doing so might cost them their reputation, influence or standing within their circles. We should consider what that reveals about our understanding of sacrifice.

Pastors and Christian leaders know the pressure to avoid controversy. Biblical teaching can offend cultural sensibilities, challenge prevailing assumptions or invite criticism. Yet Hebrews 4:12 (KJV) reminds us that "the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword."

SOUTHERN BAPTIST PRESIDENT CALLS ON PASTORS TO 'STEP UP' AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Scripture was never intended to conform to the prevailing opinions of the culture, but to penetrate the hearts and consciences of those who hear it. The temptation is to soften the message, avoid difficult subjects and preserve comfort through silence. Yet Christian leadership has never been about making faith comfortable. It is about proclaiming biblical truth without compromise, equipping believers to live faithfully and preparing the next generation to understand the convictions entrusted to them.

The church cannot fulfill that responsibility by retreating from questions shaping American life. Christian communicators, whether standing behind a pulpit, speaking into a microphone or reaching audiences through digital media, must communicate truth with clarity and courage. The platforms may change, but our responsibility to pass on what we have received does not.

EXCLUSIVE: NEW CHURCH CAMPAIGN SAYS AMERICA'S FAMILY CRISIS WON'T BE SOLVED BY POLITICS, BUT BY PASTORS

November's elections will determine who holds political power for a season. They will not determine whether parents teach their children the value of freedom, pastors faithfully proclaim Scripture or Christians sacrifice their comfort for future generations. Those responsibilities cannot be delegated to Washington, nor do they disappear when an election ends.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The American Dream was never meant to be a purely personal arrangement, a private guarantee that each of us, in our own lifetime, could claim "Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness" for ourselves alone. It was always a longer promise: a commitment to build and keep a country in which those same freedoms and opportunities would remain available to the generations who follow.

We enjoy the possibility of that dream because earlier Americans treated it as something worth protecting beyond their own lifetimes. They understood that the real measure of the work was not only what they could enjoy, but what they left standing for those who had not yet arrived. In that sense, the dream was never finished in any single generation; it was entrusted, again and again, to the next.

item.title: People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits
item.description: National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.
item.content:encoded:
National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.

In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.

PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS

A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.

The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.

Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.

The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.

AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED

"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."

The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."

Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.

GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."

As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.

"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."

Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.

DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT

"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.

In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.

Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.

"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."

Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.

"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."

Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.

Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.

"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

item.title: NFL's dumbest moment of the week once again welcomes Jets coach Aaron Glenn, who is on the hot seat
item.description: Aaron Glenn's questionable timeout decisions let the Dolphins run nearly nine minutes off the clock before halftime in a stunning 28-25 New York Jets loss.
item.content:encoded:
When it was over, Aaron Glenn was blaming and second-guessing himself after another New York Jets loss. And this has become perhaps too familiar for the team's coach this season.

The Jets lost to the previously winless Miami Dolphins on Sunday, and while that can happen because the other guys get paid, too, the Dolphins had been getting paid without winning before this one.

In fact, the Dolphins had been getting paid without even leading a game all season.

WINLESS DOLPHINS END HISTORIC DROUGHT AND THEY DID IT AGAINST THE ALMOST-AS-HAPLESS JETS

But against Glenn's team, the Dolphins looked like a playoff contender. That left Glenn disappointed. And defeated.

"When it comes to this game, highly disappointed," Glenn lamented. "Disappointed in myself, first and foremost."

NFL'S DUMBEST MOMENT OF WEEK 2 GOES TO JETS COACH AARON GLENN WHO PLAYED NOT TO LOSE AT END OF REGULATION

Glenn is familiar with losing this season, but when the head coach is blaming himself for his clock management, that familiar spot is problematic. And that's exactly where Glenn was for the second time this season — guilty of the dumbest moment of the week.

That Week 7 moment:

The Dolphins held a 14-7 lead with 8:44 left before halftime, and then they went on the Earth's longest drive.

They marched from their own 9-yard line to the Jets 32-yard line with only two minutes remaining until half. Holding all his timeouts, Glenn stood idly on the sideline like a spectator.

'I LOST US THAT GAME': NICK SIRIANNI MAKES DECISION THAT OPENED DOOR TO A JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS COMEBACK WIN

"Yeah, I think that's one they were already down in the red zone, correct?" Glenn asked reporters who wanted an explanation. "That’s the one you’re talking about?"

Well, the Dolphins weren't in the red zone. They were at the New York 25 with 1:16 to play. But Glenn saved his timeouts for use in the year 2037, when he maybe gets his next head coaching opportunity.

So the clock ticked, and ticked and ticked, and the next time Miami ran a play, there were only 35 left on the clock.

The Dolphins eventually scored again, and the moment passed, but the clock management from the coach was curious.

"Man, we felt like we were going to stop them," Glenn said. "And maybe we should have called our timeouts to get it back, but at that point, we just felt like we were going to stop them and be able to get the ball back.

"That's something that we should have done is use our timeouts."

Yes, correct.

Glenn's explanation actually makes zero sense because if the Jets had done as he thought and held the Dolphins scoreless, using the timeouts would have given the Jets the football back with more time remaining on the clock.

As it was, the Jets got the ball back with six seconds remaining in the first half, which New York used to merely take a knee.

The second half witnessed something of a Jets rally before the Dolphins eventually prevailed 28-25, but that made the failure to a call time out more glaring because the Jets might have used that extra time in the first half to manage a field goal — which eventually was the difference in the game.

The Jets, by the way, are 2-5 and Glenn is in serious trouble. His teams are terrible just before halftime, having been outscored 107-6 in the coach's 24 games.

And owner Woody Johnson has not given Glenn a vote of confidence like he did at this stage in the 2025 season. Johnson declined to speak with reporters at the League Fall Meeting last week.

"We all have to get better, from coaching to playing to everything that we’re doing, we have to get better," Glenn said. "... We know what’s going to happen from the outside in, we accept that, and it is what it is.

"This is a time where our guys, we’ve got to lock arms to make sure that everything that we get as far as energy and connection is going to be built from within, and we understand that.

"But we’ve got to play better, and our fans deserve better than that, and that starts with me."

If Glenn continues to mismanage the clock, a coaching change is going to start with him.

item.title: WWE star Drew McIntyre offers sobering reminder amid spate of deaths to hit pro wrestling world
item.description: Drew McIntyre mourns the deaths of PAC, Rick the Sign Guy, and Dennis Haskins, sharing personal memories of all three men from his WWE career.
item.content:encoded:
The pro wrestling world has been hit hard with deaths over the last few weeks.

Benjamin Satterley, the former WWE and All Elite Wrestling (AEW) star, Rick Achberger, a WWE superfan lovingly known as "Rick the Sign Guy," and former "Saved by the Bell" star Dennis Haskins, who was involved in some WWE storylines, all died within weeks of each other.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

WWE star Drew McIntyre, who is in the micro-drama series "Agent of Shadows," told OutKick Dropkick to "remember to tell the ones you love, you love them" as he mourned the loss of all three men.

"I remember him as the best of us," McIntyre said of Satterley. "He was so positive all the time to everybody around him in an industry where you can be negative at times. He was unbelievable in the ring. He never ever changed. I've seen him from day one of his career, fresh out the backyard, in a company called 3CW in Carlisle, England, he'd literally just started wrestling there fresh in the backyard, and I was told wait till you see Pac, and I was a teenager at the time, and my mind was blown. I'd never seen anyone so precise, so accurate, so unbelievable, and such a nice guy, and we traveled to Ireland together, went to London together.

"We used to tell each other, hey, I was like man, you're the one that's going to break out from the U.K., he'd tell me the same thing, and to see how far he came, the career he had, and, most importantly, the person he was the whole time was amazing and you've seen the response online that tells to the character of the man."

McIntyre spoke with OutKick Dropkick before he put out his video tribute of Satterley. He added that Satterley’s legacy extended beyond the ring because of the man he was.

"I've tried to write things, I even tried to do a video and it just, I don't know, nothing felt right, it's just shocking, 40 years old," McIntyre said. "But to leave that kind of legacy, the body of work's one thing, you know, a lot of guys have got an incredible body of work in wrestling, you Google their name, not good people. I think the most important thing, Ben gets looked back on, it's crazy to think about him in the past tense, it'll be with positivity and that he really made an impact on people personally."

"And I'd have to mention my guy Rick as well." he continued. "I tried to write something about him again. He was part of our WWE family or one of our super fans. And when I was 22, came to America, get put straight on TV and live events with people like The Undertaker and Triple H and Shawn Michaels, I was terrified. The crowd did not care.

"He would get them going every time. He would get them booing me if I was a bad guy, cheering me if I was a good guy, until eventually I found my feet and then he would abuse me every time and I loved every second of it. Yeah, it's been a hard week in our industry and Mr. Belding as well, Dennis (Haskins). I used to call him Mr. B all the time. I just looked at a picture of us flipping the camera off together, it's, it's been a hard week and yeah, just remember to tell the ones you love, you love them."

Nothing hits harder than losing a loved one in your circle and no one knows that more than the pro wrestling world – especially lately.
